memory_update.text: Restaurants 2026 chokepoint appears to be margin-control rather than absolute demand: labor, beef/input costs, limited pricing power, payment fees, and technology-driven productivity are the highest-friction nodes.
Digital ordering/POS/payments/loyalty is a core enabling layer because operators need direct guest data, lower-friction ordering, menu analytics, labor productivity, and payment workflows.
Foodservice broadline distribution is a key upstream node for cost control, private-label substitution, replenishment reliability, and independent restaurant supply.
Beef-heavy restaurant concepts should be tracked separately because cattle supply constraints and high beef prices create a specific input-cost chokepoint.

Track USDA Food Price Outlook, cattle/beef outlooks, restaurant earnings, technology-vendor earnings, state wage changes, immigration policy, swipe-fee policy, and USMCA/tariff developments as the main Layer 2A catalyst set.

Need next-layer company-by-company validation of restaurant-level margins, traffic versus price mix, franchisee economics, loyalty engagement, delivery mix, wage exposure by state, and commodity hedging or purchasing arrangements.

Need market-pricing check in Layer 2B/3: compare restaurant operators, delivery marketplaces, POS/software vendors, distributors, and equipment suppliers on valuation, earnings revisions, traffic data, and margin trajectory; no buy/sell view has been formed.
MCD should be tracked as the franchised global QSR value/loyalty benchmark; key falsifier is loyalty/value growth that relies on discounting while guest traffic or franchisee economics weaken.

TOST is the clearest restaurant-tech chokepoint in this chunk because its GPV, location count, and module adoption can indicate whether operators keep funding POS, payments, loyalty, labor, and analytics tools under cost pressure.
DASH and UBER are delivery/off-premises nodes, but restaurant-specific signal is diluted by expansion into grocery, convenience, retail, ads, international platforms, and mobility in Uber's case.
SYY and PFGC are upstream distribution read-throughs for restaurant volume, independent restaurant health, input inflation, and private-label/menu-cost mitigation.
TXRH and DRI are useful casual-dining tests for whether experiential/value perception can offset food and labor inflation; beef exposure is especially important for TXRH and DRI's LongHorn.

CAVA and CMG are fast-casual tests moving in opposite evidence directions: CAVA still has unit-growth strength but traffic normalization risk, while CMG's 2025 comparable sales decline is a clear falsification signal for premium fast-casual resilience.
SBUX is a beverage/coffee traffic-recovery and throughput test; 2025 transaction declines mean the key issue is not simply brand scale but whether operational changes restore visit frequency.
Need current 2026 quarterly evidence for all tickers: traffic vs price/mix, promotional intensity, loyalty active users, labor productivity, commodity pass-through, and restaurant-level margin.

Need valuation and market-pricing layer later: estimate revisions, same-store-sales expectations, margin expectations, short interest, EV/EBITDA or sales multiples, and whether strong narratives are already priced.
Need franchisee-level evidence for MCD and YUM, including franchisee cash flow, remodel obligations, closures, development commitments, royalty/ad-fund burden, and access to financing.
EAT is a high-signal operator mapping for casual-dining value, Chili's traffic, menu simplification, and margin durability; validate through traffic/price/mix and promotion intensity.

PAR and OLO are the purest restaurant-technology mappings in this chunk; PAR has broader POS/engagement/hardware exposure, while OLO is more concentrated in ordering, payments, delivery orchestration, and guest engagement.

MIDD maps to restaurant capex, throughput, kitchen automation, beverage, and refrigeration equipment, but restaurant-specific exposure must be separated from other commercial and institutional foodservice demand.

QSR, DPZ, WING, and WEN should be tracked as franchised-system unit-economics reads rather than only consumer-demand reads; key variables are franchisee margins, remodel obligations, traffic, price/mix, and net unit growth.
USFD is a broadline foodservice-distribution mapping; independent restaurant case volume is a useful proxy for restaurant demand and operator health.

BROS and SHAK are growth-concept mappings: BROS tests beverage frequency and drive-thru throughput, while SHAK tests premium fast-casual traffic, beef/labor cost pressure, and restaurant-level margin improvement.

WBT should be removed from the active public ticker universe because Welbilt is no longer a standalone public company after the Ali Group acquisition; rebuild the equipment node using active listed peers.

Need market-pricing checks for all tickers before prioritization: forward EV/EBITDA or P/E, same-store-sales expectations, estimate revisions, short interest, and relative performance versus restaurant and supplier peers.

Need a common restaurant KPI table across operator tickers: traffic, average check, price/mix, comparable sales, restaurant-level margin, labor cost, food/paper cost, net unit growth, franchised mix, and franchisee health indicators.
Correct Sweetgreen ticker from SGV to SG in the restaurant theme universe; SG maps to fast-casual demand, restaurant-level profitability, and Infinite Kitchen automation.
Retire PTVE as an active public ticker in restaurant packaging mapping because Pactiv Evergreen was acquired by Novolex and delisted in 2025.
Retire BERY as a standalone active public ticker and remap any Berry Global foodservice-packaging exposure to AMCR after the Amcor-Berry combination.

Keep WING only once in the dashboard universe; this chunk's WING entry is a duplicate, but the relationship remains relevant to franchised chicken QSR, digital ordering, and chicken input sensitivity.

DNUT's McDonald's expansion catalyst should be downgraded or removed; post-July 2, 2025 mapping should focus on grocery/high-volume retail distribution, international franchising, route density, and debt/liquidity.
JACK should be tracked as a turnaround/value-QSR and franchisee-health case, with closures and same-store-sales declines as primary falsification variables.
BLMN maps strongly to steakhouse/beef sensitivity and casual-dining turnaround; Outback traffic and beef/input costs are key evidence nodes.
ARCO is a high-purity public mapping for McDonald's operator-level economics in Latin America, distinct from MCD's asset-light franchisor exposure.
Need current quarter same-store-sales and traffic-versus-price decomposition for CAKE, DIN, BLMN, JACK, PZZA, SG, WING, and ARCO before assigning Layer 3 priority.
Need restaurant-specific revenue exposure for TSN protein supply and AMCR/Berry packaging before treating them as high-purity restaurant supply-chain tickers.
Need franchisee-level economics where available: unit closures, remodel obligations, royalty burden, rent, debt availability, labor costs, and promotional funding for DIN, JACK, PZZA, WING, and ARCO.
PPC upgraded within restaurant-adjacent input suppliers: direct QSR link is supported by 2025 company commentary on Small Bird strength in QSR and foodservice distribution.
HRL validated as a prepared-foods and foodservice input supplier; restaurant exposure exists but is blended with other food-away-from-home channels, so purity remains medium.

ARMK validated as an adjacent institutional foodservice/operator benchmark for away-from-home demand, procurement scale, labor intensity, and distributor relationships, not as a pure restaurant-chain play.
SODEY validated as a global contract-catering and food-services benchmark; relationship to Restaurants theme is adjacent and international, with ADR/listing validation still needed.

Need customer concentration and restaurant-specific revenue exposure for PPC and HRL; both companies disclose foodservice/QSR relationships, but not a clean restaurant-chain revenue percentage in the evidence reviewed.

Need margin pass-through analysis across PPC, HRL, ARMK, and SODEY: contract structure, commodity pass-through clauses, vendor rebates, and pricing lag are more important than headline revenue growth.

Need current market-pricing checks for all four tickers before prioritization: valuation, estimate revisions, short interest, commodity expectations, and consensus assumptions are not included in Layer 2B mapping.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Initial Serenity Layer 2A map for the Restaurants theme: the industry chain is currently shaped less by pure unit-growth scarcity and more by a margin-control chokepoint. The highest-friction nodes are labor availability/productivity, beef and other food-input inflation, value-menu/menu-engineering capability, digital ordering/POS/loyalty infrastructure, payment/interchange costs, and foodservice distribution scale. Consumer demand remains large, but 2026 evidence points to cautious household spending, uneven traffic, and a limited ability for operators to keep raising prices. This is a research map only, not a security recommendation.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurants depend on repeat traffic, but 2026 evidence indicates restrained consumer spending, uneven traffic, and stronger sensitivity to discounts, loyalty, and everyday value. This node determines whether operators can grow sales through visits rather than only through price.

supply_chain_map.node: Menu pricing ceiling and menu engineering
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: After several years of inflation, many operators appear to have less room to raise menu prices without damaging traffic or profits. This raises the importance of menu mix, portion design, protein substitution, bundles, value meals, beverages, and promotions.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant labor availability and wage inflation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Foodservice is labor-intensive. Staffing shortages, higher wage floors, immigration enforcement uncertainty, and training needs can cap store hours, service quality, new-unit openings, and restaurant-level margins.

Operators need ordering, payments, kiosks, handhelds, back-office tools, scheduling, AI/data analytics, and automation to offset wage pressure and free staff for hospitality. This node links restaurant demand to software and equipment suppliers.

supply_chain_map.node: Digital ordering, payments, POS, loyalty, and guest data
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Direct digital channels, loyalty programs, and integrated payment/POS systems help operators influence frequency, manage menus, reduce friction, analyze demand, and reduce dependence on third-party delivery economics.

Off-premises demand remains structurally important, especially for younger consumers, but delivery commissions and channel economics can pressure restaurant margins. Scale, density, and subscription engagement matter for marketplace operators.

Broadline distributors aggregate purchasing, cold-chain logistics, private-label inputs, replenishment, and chain/independent restaurant supply. Distribution scale becomes more important when operators need cost control and reliable input availability.

Beef remains a high-friction input because cattle supply cannot recover quickly. Beef-heavy casual dining, burger, and steak concepts may face higher food-cost pressure, while chicken, pork, plant-forward, and beverage-led menus may gain relative flexibility.

supply_chain_map.node: Eggs, dairy, coffee, poultry, produce, packaging, and other food inputs
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Non-beef inputs influence segment margins differently: coffee affects beverage concepts, eggs affect breakfast, poultry affects chicken QSR, produce affects fast casual, and packaging affects off-premises economics. Input volatility can create brand-level divergence.

supply_chain_map.node: Commercial kitchen, beverage, refrigeration, and automation equipment
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Equipment that improves throughput, cooking consistency, labor productivity, beverage programs, and energy efficiency can become more valuable as operators seek margin relief without degrading guest experience.

Franchise-heavy QSR systems depend on franchisee cash flow to fund remodels, new units, value-menu promotions, technology upgrades, and labor investments. If franchisee margins compress, brand-level growth and marketing flexibility may weaken.

supply_chain_map.node: Beverage innovation and non-alcoholic beverage mix
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Beverages can carry attractive margins, drive visits, support daypart expansion, and offset pressure in food-heavy categories. 2026 industry commentary highlights drinks as a traffic driver and non-alcoholic beverages as a key consumer trend.

supply_chain_map.node: Payment/interchange fees and card acceptance costs
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Card fees are a major operating expense after food and labor for many operators. Policy changes around interchange fees can alter margin pressure, especially for smaller independent restaurants with less negotiating power.

supply_chain_map.node: Immigration policy and work authorization pipeline
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurants rely heavily on immigrant labor. Enforcement intensity or reform can directly affect staffing availability, wage pressure, store hours, service quality, and expansion plans.

supply_chain_map.node: Tariffs, USMCA review, packaging, steel, aluminum, and equipment costs
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Trade policy can raise costs for food inputs, packaging, equipment, and imported goods. The 2026 USMCA review and tariff environment are watch items for supply-chain and capex cost pressure.

Restaurants in fine dining, urban, resort, airport, and tourism-heavy markets are exposed to domestic and international travel flows. This node can create regional divergence even if national restaurant sales grow.
